subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 9 periods = 405 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 45min

periods.activity_title: Entering the World of the Magnifying Glass

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.221): paired pre-reading discussion on magnification pictures.
Let us read (p.221): share what you would use a magnifying glass for.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays or describes the pictures of people using magnifying glasses from the textbook. In pairs, students discuss what is common across the pictures and which instruments they recognise.

Teacher reads the poem “Magnifying Glass” aloud at an unhurried pace while students follow in their books. After the read-aloud, the class pauses briefly on any unfamiliar words or vivid images that caught attention.

Students re-read the poem silently, then share with a partner which instruments they know that magnify objects and why those in the pictures need such tools. A few pairs share responses with the whole class.

Students respond briefly to the open prompt: if you had a magnifying glass right now, what would you examine and why? Two or three volunteers share their answers aloud, building curiosity for the deeper textual work ahead.

periods.teacher_notes: The pre-reading images of people using magnifying glasses serve as the bridge into the poem’s central wonder—ordinary objects made extraordinary through a lens. A common pitfall is rushing past the poem’s playful tone; encourage students to notice the speaker’s delight and surprise in phrases like “Magic talk” and “tigerish claws” before any analytical work begins. The suffix activity on page 226 (adding ‘-ish’ to nouns) is not covered in this sitting and makes a good self-study word-play exercise.
materials: Blackboard or display space for key vocabulary

periods.activity_title: Reading the Poem for Meaning and Structure

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.223): complete poem summary using words from the poem.
Let us discuss (p.223): fill blanks on main idea, tone, stanza form, and rhyme scheme.

time_bands.activity: Teacher re-reads the poem stanza by stanza aloud, pausing after each stanza for students to name what the speaker observes and what strikes them as surprising or vivid.

Students work individually on the poem summary cloze task on page 223, selecting words from the poem to fill in eight blanks. Teacher circulates and prompts students who are stuck by asking them to re-read the relevant stanza.

Class completes the four fill-in-the-bracket questions on main idea, tone, stanza count, and rhyme scheme as a shared discussion, with the teacher guiding students to count stanzas and lines, and trace the ABCB pattern aloud together.
Teacher consolidates: names the six-stanza, four-line-each structure and the ABCB rhyme scheme on the board, then asks students to say in one word the emotion the poet wants the reader to feel.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem aloud together, students are now ready to examine its architecture. A frequent misconception is that the rhyme scheme is ABCD because not every pair rhymes identically; direct students to the second and fourth lines of each stanza to confirm the ABCB pattern. The reflective ECR questions on page 225 (speaker’s attitude towards nature, favourite part) are substantive and best reserved for later in-class discussion rather than this structural sitting.

periods.activity_title: Poetic Devices and Imagery in the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.223): identify examples of simile, alliteration, and metaphor.
Let us think and reflect (p.224): explain visual imagery in chalk and moss lines.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.224): complete four sentence-completion questions on exclamation marks, personification, repetitive pattern, and the moon stanza.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly introduces the three poetic devices—simile, alliteration, metaphor—with one fresh example for each written on the board, before inviting students to hunt for them in the poem.

Students work in pairs to locate and write one example each of simile, alliteration, and metaphor from the poem. Pairs share their answers; the teacher confirms “Like hive of bees” (simile), “woven web-silk” (alliteration), and “Magic talk” (metaphor) on the board.

Class turns to the visual imagery questions on page 224. Teacher reads the stem about “A myriad shells show in a scrap of chalk” and “A forest—flowers and trees,” then students discuss in pairs what the magnifying glass reveals and what the forest comparison emphasises. Selected responses are shared aloud.

Teacher closes by connecting the devices to the poem’s theme: each literary device intensifies the sense of wonder, turning plain objects into marvels. Students note this theme-device link in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem’s imagery is densely layered; students often label any comparison as a simile—guide them to check for the presence of “like” or “as.” For metaphor, “Magic talk” requires the recognition that the magnifying glass is being personified as well as metaphorically characterised, which is worth unpacking. The four sentence-completion questions on page 224 about exclamation marks, personification, the stanza pattern, and the moon stanza are set as homework to allow deeper reflection time.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.224): extract-based true/false, line selection, comparison question, and MCQ on poet’s feeling.
Let us think and reflect (p.225): significance of the spider, and why the poem ends with the moon.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Extract 1 from page 224 aloud; students follow in their books. Class works on the true/false question about magical powers, the line-selection question about intricate patterns, and the MCQ on the poet’s feeling—students answer individually, then discuss answers as a class.

Students write a short response to the comparison question: what does calling “an inch of moss” a “forest” suggest about the speaker’s view? Two or three responses are shared and the class refines the idea that the lens makes the minute feel immense.

Class moves to page 225 for the two short-answer questions: the significance of the spider stanza (tigerish claws, multifaceted eyes, predatory detail) and why the poem ends with the moon. Students discuss in pairs before writing their answers.

Teacher consolidates the progression from tiny natural objects (chalk, moss, water, spider) to a celestial body, underscoring the poem’s central argument that lenses infinitely expand human perception.

periods.teacher_notes: Having examined the poem’s devices and imagery, students are now equipped to read the extract analytically. Watch for students who answer the true/false question by agreeing that the poet has magical powers—the glass is the “magic,” not a supernatural ability. The two reflective ECR questions on page 225 (how the speaker’s view would change without the lens; the speaker’s attitude to nature) require extended writing and are best reserved for a writing-focused sitting rather than this analytical discussion.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Indian Inventions; Speaking About Sound

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.227): mark four true statements from six about father-daughter conversation on Indian inventions.
Let us speak (p.225): read words with /v/ and /f/ sounds aloud with teacher guidance.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the listening task context: a father and daughter discussing lesser-known Indian inventions. Students read the six statements on page 227 silently before listening begins, so they know what to listen for.

Teacher reads the transcript aloud at a natural conversational pace. Students listen and mark which four of the six statements they believe to be true. Teacher reads the transcript a second time at a slightly slower pace; students may revise their markings.

Class discusses each statement in turn, with students justifying their true/false judgements by recalling specific details from the conversation. Teacher confirms the four true statements and highlights the reasoning behind each.

Teacher models the /f/ and /v/ sounds, explaining the lip-and-teeth placement. Students practise the words listed on the speaking page—“forest,” “deft,” “hive,” “woven,” “marvellous” and others—in chorus, then individually.

Teacher reads a sentence or two from the poem aloud, deliberately placing /f/ and /v/ words, and asks volunteers to identify them. Students then read the same lines aloud, focusing on accurate consonant articulation.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening transcript features a natural, informal register; remind students that in real conversation speakers express both surprise and confirmation, and that emotional response (the father’s delight, the daughter’s pride) is itself information for judging the statements. For the /v/ and /f/ distinction, students whose first language does not contrast these sounds may need extra modelling; focus on the lower-lip contact with the upper teeth rather than voice quality alone. The two imaginative speaking tasks (space travel and wonder invention) are rich extended activities that each need their own generous time allocation and are taken up in the next speaking sitting.

periods.activity_title: Speaking About Space Travel and Wonder Inventions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.228): speak about a chosen planet for space travel and five things to take along.
Let us speak (p.228): describe a self-chosen wonder invention with reasons.

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets the context of both speaking tasks, writing key guiding prompts on the board: which planet, why, five preparations for space; and what the invention is, how it works, and why it matters.

Students spend time individually organising their ideas for the space-travel task on a rough note. They then practise their response quietly before delivering it to a partner. Two or three volunteers present to the class.

Students shift to the wonder-invention task, again planning their ideas briefly before a paired practice. The teacher circulates, encouraging students to give specific reasons for their invention choice rather than vague claims.
Three or four volunteers present their wonder invention to the class. The class listens and is invited to ask one question each to the speaker, practising attentive listening alongside speaking.
Teacher closes by connecting both tasks to the poem’s theme: the magnifying glass was itself a wonder invention that expanded human vision; curiosity drives both science and imagination.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem’s final stanza—imagining the moon within walking distance through a lens—provides a natural conceptual bridge to the space-travel speaking task. Encourage students who are hesitant to speak by reminding them that an informal planning note is welcome; the goal is expressing curiosity clearly, not perfection of delivery. The writing task on dialogue between Deepa and Asma is taken up in the next sitting and should not be previewed here.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.228): draft a full dialogue between Deepa and Asma about a Science Fair model.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the given conversation starter aloud (Deepa’s opening and Asma’s hesitant response) and discusses the five ‘points to remember’: setting, tone, key information, emotion brackets, and filler words. Sample lines are written on the board to illustrate informal dialogue formatting.

Students plan their dialogue in note form—deciding the setting, the model Deepa and Asma might propose, a point of disagreement and how they resolve it—before writing their first draft. Teacher circulates, checking that students include emotion/action brackets and at least one filler word.

Students exchange drafts with a partner for a brief peer response: the partner checks whether the dialogue has a clear setting, shows both agreement and disagreement, and uses the formatting conventions. Students note one suggestion for revision.
Students revise their draft based on the peer response, then two pairs read their conversations aloud to the class. Teacher highlights strong uses of emotion brackets and filler words as models.

periods.teacher_notes: Dialogue writing calls on awareness of register—here informal but purposeful, between classmates planning a science project. A common pitfall is producing an exchange that is too formal or too sparse; the ‘points to remember’ on page 228 are explicit scaffolds and worth keeping visible on the board throughout. Because the entire cycle of planning, drafting, peer response, and revision happens inside this sitting, no written artefact from an earlier sitting is needed or assumed.

periods.activity_title: Vocabulary from the Poem: Words, Idioms, and Suffixes

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.225): fill blanks in paragraph using six words from the poem—woven, myriad, deft, stumble, surpass, marvellous.
Let us learn (p.226): match collective noun phrases to correct words.
Let us learn (p.226): match ‘eye’ idioms to their meanings.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.226): choose nouns from the list that take the suffix ‘-ish’ to make adjectives.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the six poem words on the board—“woven, myriad, deft, stumble, surpass, marvellous”—and asks students to predict each word’s meaning from its use in the poem before the paragraph task begins.

Students work individually on the fill-in-the-blanks paragraph on page 225, choosing the correct word for each gap. Teacher facilitates a class check, asking students to justify their choices by referring back to how the word was used in the poem.

Class tackles the collective nouns matching task on page 226. Teacher reads each phrase aloud—“a swarm of,” “a constellation of,” “a grove of” and so on—and students match them to the words in Column 2 before comparing answers with a partner.

Students work on the ‘eye’ idioms matching task on page 226, using context and, where needed, a dictionary. Teacher confirms answers, then invites students to use two of the idioms in spoken sentences describing something from the poem or classroom life.
Teacher sets the suffix ‘-ish’ task from page 226 as a brief home exploration, reminding students to try each noun from the list and decide which ones produce a real English adjective.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem supplies the exact context for all six vocabulary words, making prediction from the verse a natural first step before the paragraph task. Students sometimes confuse “surpass” (to exceed) with “surface” or “surpass itself” with a reflexive contradiction—read the poem line “And itself surpass” aloud to clarify that the tiny thing, magnified, exceeds its own apparent scale. The suffix ‘-ish’ exploration is assigned home work because it is a word-play task best done with a little unhurried trial and error.

periods.activity_title: Exploring Telescopes, Observatories, and Ancient Indian Astronomy

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.229): read and discuss India’s major telescopes and world observatories.
Let us explore (p.229): read about ancient Indian astronomers—Āryabhaṭa, Varāmihira, Bhāskaracārya II.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore (p.229): read about Jantar Mantar and its five observatory sites across India.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects the poem’s final stanza—where lenses bring the moon within reach—to the idea of telescopes. Class reads the descriptions of ARIES (Nainital), the Indian Astronomical Observatory (Hanle, Ladakh), the James Webb Space Telescope, and Mauna Kea Observatory from the textbook together.

Students discuss in small groups: how does each telescope extend the human eye in a way the poem’s magnifying glass metaphorically suggested? Groups share one observation each; teacher records key points on the board.

Class reads about the three ancient Indian astronomers—Āryabhaṭa, Varāmihira, and Bhāskaracārya II—and their texts. Teacher asks: what does it tell us about curiosity and observation that these scholars were doing astronomical work more than a thousand years ago?

Students write three sentences connecting the theme of the poem (wonder and observation through lenses) to at least one telescope or one ancient scholar they have just read about. Two or three sentences are shared aloud.
Teacher sets the Jantar Mantar reading from page 229 as a home exploration, inviting students to find out which of the five observatory cities is nearest to them.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem’s assertion that lenses could bring the moon within walking distance is the conceptual springboard for this sitting—grounding the beyond-text work in the verse itself keeps the interdisciplinary connection visible. Students may be surprised that India had serious observational astronomy in the sixth century CE; use this as an opportunity to discuss how curiosity is not modern but deeply human. The Jantar Mantar reading is assigned as home exploration because it works well as individual investigation rather than class-time reading.
materials: Internet access if available for telescope images

items.source_lo: Student analyses how poetic language, structure, and imagery create meaning using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Walter de la Mare’s poem; magnifying glass as wonder; simile, alliteration, metaphor, visual imagery, stanza structure, ABCB rhyme, exclamation marks, celestial extension in final stanza.
items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 222 beginning “With this round glass.” Which of the following best describes the effect of the magnifying glass on the speaker in the poem?

options.label: A
options.text: It makes the speaker feel frightened by the hidden complexity of ordinary things.

options.label: B
options.text: It fills the speaker with wonder by revealing intricate detail in everyday objects.

options.label: C
options.text: It convinces the speaker that nature is too small to be worth studying.

options.label: D
options.text: It makes the speaker feel that science has replaced imagination entirely.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the student is misreading the poem’s tone of delight as one of anxiety or alarm.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals a reversal of the poem’s argument—the lens magnifies, not diminishes, the value of small things.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Introduces a science-versus-imagination opposition the poem does not make; the glass unites both.

items.source_lo: Student analyses how poetic language, structure, and imagery create meaning using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Walter de la Mare’s poem; magnifying glass as wonder; simile, alliteration, metaphor, visual imagery, stanza structure, ABCB rhyme, exclamation marks, celestial extension in final stanza.
items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 222 beginning “Yes, and with lenses like it.” The final stanza moves from tiny natural objects—chalk, moss, a drop of water, a spider’s web—to the moon. What does this shift suggest about the poet’s view of scientific instruments and human curiosity? Support your answer with a detail from an earlier stanza of the poem.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The shift to the moon suggests that lenses do not merely magnify the immediately visible but extend human perception without limit—curiosity, armed with the right instrument, can reach the celestial. An earlier stanza supports this: a drop of water teeming “like hive of bees” shows the same principle at a microscopic scale, establishing that every lens, however small, dissolves the boundary between the ordinary and the vast.

items.source_lo: Student evaluates the accuracy and emotional tone of spoken information using a listening conversation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Father-daughter conversation on lesser-known Indian inventions: Jagadish Chandra Bose (radio), Narinder Kapany (fibre optics), Snakes and Ladders, Ajay Bhatt (USB).
items.item_stem: Listen to the conversation between the father and daughter. Which of the following statements about the father is accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The father already knew that Narinder Kapany pioneered fibre optics.

options.label: B
options.text: The father contributed a new invention fact to the conversation that the daughter had not mentioned.

options.label: C
options.text: The father expressed disappointment that so few inventions came from India.

options.label: D
options.text: The father believed Marconi deserved full credit for radio broadcasting.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the student missed the father’s admission that he only had a vague idea fibre optics had Indian roots.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Contradicts the conversation’s overall celebratory tone; the father says he ‘definitely learned a lot.’
what_each_option_reveals.D: The father does not defend Marconi; he simply expresses surprise that Bose preceded him.

items.source_lo: Student evaluates the accuracy and emotional tone of spoken information using a listening conversation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Father-daughter conversation on lesser-known Indian inventions: Jagadish Chandra Bose (radio), Narinder Kapany (fibre optics), Snakes and Ladders, Ajay Bhatt (USB).
items.item_stem:
After listening to the conversation, a student wrote the following notes. Identify whether each statement is true or false based on what was said in the conversation.
1. Narinder Kapany was a physicist from Punjab and is known as the father of fibre optics.
2. Snakes and Ladders was originally invented purely as an entertaining board game with no moral meaning.
3. The daughter expressed amazement when her father mentioned the USB port.
4. Jagadish Chandra Bose conducted microwave experiments before Marconi demonstrated radio broadcasting.

options.text: Narinder Kapany was a physicist from Punjab and is known as the father of fibre optics.
Snakes and Ladders was originally invented purely as an entertaining board game with no moral meaning.
The daughter expressed amazement when her father mentioned the USB port.
Jagadish Chandra Bose conducted microwave experiments before Marconi demonstrated radio broadcasting.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — the daughter states Narinder Kapany was an Indian physicist from Punjab and calls him ‘the father of fibre optics.’
2. False — the daughter explains the game had a spiritual meaning and was invented to teach children values, with ladders representing virtues and snakes representing evil.
3. True — the daughter says ‘That’s amazing’ and remarks she cannot imagine life without USB.
4. True — the daughter says Jagadish Chandra Bose conducted an experiment using microwaves before Marconi.

items.source_lo: Student communicates ideas with reasons and imagination using oral presentation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Pronunciation of /v/ and /f/ consonants; imagined space travel to a planet; inventing a wonder device—both tasks linked to the poem’s theme of curiosity and discovery.
items.item_stem: The poem ‘Magnifying Glass’ ends with the idea that lenses could make the moon seem within walking distance. Describe in two to three spoken sentences which planet you would most like to visit and give one clear reason why. Also name two things you would take with you on the journey.

expected_elements: Names a specific planet and states one clear reason for the choice.
Names two relevant items to take on the journey.
Speaks in complete sentences with a connected sequence of ideas.
Maintains a conversational but focused tone throughout.

items.source_lo: Student communicates ideas with reasons and imagination using oral presentation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Pronunciation of /v/ and /f/ consonants; imagined space travel to a planet; inventing a wonder device—both tasks linked to the poem’s theme of curiosity and discovery.
items.item_stem: The poet says his magnifying glass can ‘make Magic talk’ by revealing wonders invisible to the naked eye. Imagine you have invented a new scientific device that extends human perception in any direction—sight, sound, time, or another sense. In a short spoken response of four to five sentences, describe what your device does, explain why it matters, and give your opinion on how it might change the way people understand the world around them.

expected_elements: Describes the device’s function clearly and originally.
Explains why the invention matters with a specific reason.
Offers a personal opinion on its broader impact on human understanding.
Uses four to five connected sentences with appropriate vocabulary.

items.source_lo: Student drafts purposeful dialogue with appropriate register, structure, and conventions using guided writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Informal conversation between two Science Club members, Deepa and Asma, planning a Science Fair model; includes setting, tone, agreement/disagreement, emotion brackets, and filler words.
items.item_stem: Deepa and Asma are Science Club members deciding on a model for the upcoming Science Fair. Write a short conversation of six to eight exchanges between them. Your dialogue must: show where and when they are talking; include at least one point of disagreement and one of agreement; use emotion or action words in brackets at least twice; include at least one filler word such as ‘Ugh,’ ‘Er…’ or ‘Uff.’ You may begin with: Deepa: Hi Asma! Our Science teacher mentioned that you have a wonderful idea for the Science Fair project. Asma: (hesitatingly) Yes, I do. But I’m not sure if it is good enough.

expected_elements: Sets the time and place clearly within the opening exchange.
Includes one clear point of disagreement and one of agreement.
Uses at least two bracketed emotion or action words correctly.
Maintains an informal but purposeful register throughout.

items.source_lo: Student drafts purposeful dialogue with appropriate register, structure, and conventions using guided writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Informal conversation between two Science Club members, Deepa and Asma, planning a Science Fair model; includes setting, tone, agreement/disagreement, emotion brackets, and filler words.
items.item_stem: After successfully making their Science Fair model, Deepa and Asma present it to their teacher. The teacher asks them why they chose this particular model and whether they faced any difficulties. Write the conversation between the three of them—Deepa, Asma, and the teacher. Your writing should show the shift in register when students speak to a teacher compared with how they spoke to each other, and should reveal each character’s personality through their word choices and responses.

expected_elements: Shifts register noticeably when students address the teacher versus each other.
Reveals at least two characters’ personalities through word choice.
Explains the model choice and acknowledges a difficulty faced.
Uses dialogue formatting conventions consistently throughout.

items.source_lo: Student applies vocabulary in context and identifies word-formation and idiomatic patterns using a poem’s language as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Six poem words (woven, myriad, deft, stumble, surpass, marvellous); collective nouns; ‘eye’ idioms; suffix ‘-ish’ for adjective formation.
items.item_stem: Match each word from the poem in Column A with its closest meaning in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Column A | Column B |
|---|---|
| myriad | skilful and quick |
| deft | countless; a very large number |
| surpass | to go beyond; to exceed |
| marvellous | stumbling accidentally upon something |
| stumble | causing great wonder or admiration |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: myriad – countless; a very large number, deft – skilful and quick, surpass – to go beyond; to exceed, marvellous – causing great wonder or admiration, stumble – stumbling accidentally upon something

items.source_lo: Student applies vocabulary in context and identifies word-formation and idiomatic patterns using a poem’s language as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Six poem words (woven, myriad, deft, stumble, surpass, marvellous); collective nouns; ‘eye’ idioms; suffix ‘-ish’ for adjective formation.
items.item_stem: The poem uses the phrase ‘eyeing the moon’ and the adjective ‘tigerish.’ Using your understanding of how these words work, answer the following two questions in one sentence each. (a) Choose the ‘eye’ idiom—either ‘turn a blind eye’ or ‘keep an eye on’—that better describes the speaker’s attitude towards the tiny creatures in the poem, and explain why. (b) The word ‘tigerish’ is formed by adding ‘-ish’ to a noun. Name one other noun from the poem’s world—an object, creature, or setting the poem mentions—to which you could add ‘-ish,’ and write the resulting adjective with its meaning.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (a) ‘Keep an eye on’ better describes the speaker because the poem shows the speaker lying in wait and watching the spider closely, not ignoring it. (b) Accept any plausible response grounded in the poem’s world—for example, ‘moonish’ (suggesting something pale, remote, or dreamy, like the moon the speaker imagines visiting) or ‘webish’ (suggesting something intricately net-like); the student must state the resulting adjective and a brief meaning.

items.source_context: Indian and international telescopes (ARIES, IAO Hanle, James Webb, Mauna Kea); ancient Indian astronomers (Āryabhaṭa, Varāmihira, Bhāskaracārya II); Jantar Mantar observatory.
items.item_stem:
Read the following descriptions of two observatories and then answer the question.

| Observatory | Key detail |
|---|---|
| Indian Astronomical Observatory (IAO), Hanle, Ladakh | Situated at 4,500 metres above sea level |
| ARIES, Nainital, Uttarakhand | Largest telescope in India (established 2016) |

Both observatories extend human vision far beyond what the naked eye can see, much as the magnifying glass in the poem reveals a ‘myriad shells’ in a scrap of chalk. Which of the following best explains why astronomers build observatories at very high altitudes?

options.label: A
options.text: High altitudes have less atmosphere above them, reducing distortion of starlight.

options.label: B
options.text: Telescopes are heavier than most buildings and need mountain slopes for structural support.

options.label: C

what_each_option_reveals.B: Reveals a structural misconception; telescope placement is determined by atmospheric clarity, not building engineering.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses light pollution (which is lower at altitude) with the quantity of light stars emit, which is constant.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Introduces a historical-religious link not supported by the textbook reading; the Jantar Mantar was built by a ruler for astronomical precision, not for religious proximity.

items.source_lo: Student connects a text’s central theme to real-world scientific and historical knowledge using interdisciplinary exploration as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Indian and international telescopes (ARIES, IAO Hanle, James Webb, Mauna Kea); ancient Indian astronomers (Āryabhaṭa, Varāmihira, Bhāskaracārya II); Jantar Mantar observatory.
items.item_stem: The poet Walter de la Mare imagines that with powerful lenses ‘you’d walk there in an afternoon’—a playful way of saying that instruments of observation collapse the distance between us and the distant. Choose ONE of the three ancient Indian astronomers you have read about—Āryabhaṭa, Varāmihira, or Bhāskaracārya II—and write a paragraph of five to six sentences explaining: what that scholar studied or wrote about; what tools or methods of observation might have been available to them; and how their spirit of curiosity connects to the poem’s central idea that careful observation—whether through a magnifying glass or a mathematical model—reveals a world that ‘surpasses’ ordinary sight.

expected_elements: Names the chosen scholar and identifies at least one work or discovery.
Describes an observation method or intellectual approach the scholar used.
Connects the scholar’s curiosity explicitly to the poem’s theme of wonder.
Uses five to six coherent sentences with appropriate vocabulary.
Avoids vague generalisations; anchors claims in specific details from the reading.
